Azerbaijan and Türkiye signed defense contracts worth more than $500 million in Baku on September 30. The contracts cover trainer aircraft, loitering munitions, a coastal defense system, and radars, along with an agreement to build a Turkish–Azerbaijani production facility in Nakhchivan.



The Czechoslovak Group announced a joint venture valued at 1.8 billion euros ($2.02 billion) over seven years to localize the production of self-propelled howitzers in Azerbaijan, signaling that European suppliers are also accepting Baku’s demand for technology transfer. Israel’s ARI Arms has reportedly opened a plant in the country to produce M4-type rifles.



The deals add an industrial dimension to the wider Turkish–Azerbaijani military alliance and were signed during the “Power of Unity 2026” exercise, in which Azerbaijani, Turkish, and Uzbek troops trained in Karabakh, Nakhchivan, and the Caspian Sea.

latest_rss.title: Central Asians Studying Chinese in Ever Greater Numbers
latest_rss.summary:
Executive Summary:




Ever more Central Asians are learning Chinese rather than Russian or English, convinced that Chinese is the foreign language of the future and that knowing it will help them find work with the growing number of Chinese firms and institutions in their countries.



Most Central Asians studying Chinese are doing so in Chinese-funded institutions, but a growing number are getting such instruction in local universities or from tutors, an indication that this Beijing effort at promoting its soft power in Central Asia is taking off.



At present, the numbers doing so are still relatively small compared to those studying Russian, the language of upward mobility in Soviet times, or English more recently; but they are growing rapidly and helping Beijing to cement its influence there.
